The Quiet Return of the Night Train

Two decades after the sleeper was written off, the beds are full again.

By Ines Kovacic 3 November 2024

The sleeper carriage was supposed to be finished. Budget airlines undercut it on price, high-speed lines undercut it on time, and by 2010 most European operators had quietly shunted their night stock into sidings and sold it for scrap.

That verdict has not survived contact with the last five years. Nightjet, the Austrian operator that bought much of the abandoned rolling stock, now runs sleepers to twenty-five cities and reports occupancy above ninety percent on its busiest corridors.

The economics turn on a single unusual fact: a night train sells a hotel room and a journey at the same time, which means it competes with the combined price of a short-haul flight and a night in the destination city rather than with the airfare alone.

Rolling stock remains the bottleneck. A new sleeper carriage costs several million euros and takes years to deliver, and the factories that once built them retooled long ago for commuter units. Operators are therefore rebuilding refurbished coaches from the 1990s while they wait for new orders to arrive.

The border problem

Crossing a border at midnight is still harder than it should be. Signalling systems change at the frontier, drivers must be certified for each network, and a single unstaffed junction can strand a train for an hour while a relief crew is found.

The European Union has spent a decade funding a common signalling standard, and the trains that carry the new equipment cross without stopping. The trains that do not still change locomotives in the dark, and passengers rarely notice either way.

What passengers actually book

Booking data suggests the revival is not driven by climate guilt alone. The largest growth is on routes between eight and twelve hours long, where a departure after dinner and an arrival before breakfast removes an entire travel day from the trip.

Shorter routes struggle. A six-hour sleeper arrives at four in the morning, and no amount of on-board comfort compensates for being turned out onto a cold platform before the cafes open.

Whether the revival lasts depends on whether governments keep treating track access charges as a source of revenue rather than as a lever. Night trains occupy a path for eight hours and pay for every kilometre of it, and that bill decides which routes survive the next recession.
